newsitem.title: INDIA: India rulers troubled but not shaken by WTO stand.
newsitem.headline: India rulers troubled but not shaken by WTO stand.

text.p: India's government faces trouble from its coalition partners over the country's decision to join a World Trade Organisation (WTO) accord but the protests are unlikely to unseat the government, analysts said on Sunday.

Angry lawmakers paralysed parliament on Friday after Indian government negotiators at the Singapore meeting of the WTO appeared to shift their stance over investment and labour standards by throwing their weight behind a WTO declaration.
Lawmakers from the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) and the Congress party accused the government of selling out behind parliament's back and caving in to multinationals.
The CPI-M backs Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government coalition, and Congress offers the coalition make-or-break support.

India began last week's WTO meeting by declaring it would not allow the labour issue into the final declaration from the world trade group. India also said it would not allow mention in the declaration of moves towards a multilateral investment agreement.

But it failed to keep the highly sensitive issue of labour standards out of the declaration, which also said the WTO would set up groups to study the connections between trade and investment and trade and competition.
Analysts said the objections did not pose a serious threat to the future of Deve Gowda's six-month-old government.

"They (Congress and the CPI-M) could combine forces to defeat a specific decision of the government but not to bring down the government," analyst Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research (CPR) told Reuters.
"This is an issue of policy which they cannot convert into an attempt for unseating the government," he said.
"Either party can take it to the people, but only when the time comes for going to the people. (The time) is not going to be determined by a Singapore ministerial meeting," he added.
Indian officials, who earlier opposed any attempt to place overseas investment within the ambit of the WTO, said they had only agreed to a study, not a proposed accord, on investment.

On labour standards, they said India's position was not compromised since negotiators had stalled Western attempts, seen as protectionist by New Delhi, to link trade with labour practices in developing countries.
The government was to make a statement in parliament on Monday to explain its stand at Singapore.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri told the Press Trust of India in an interview published on Sunday that his party had no plans to topple Deve Gowda's United Front (UF) government.

"We will reconsider extending support to the UF government only when it does something which totally goes against the ideology of the Congress and there is a conflict," he said. "It is too early to say such a conflict has arisen."
The CPI-M's politburo said in a statement on Saturday that the WTO declaration could lead to an agreement that would spur investments harmful to Indian interests.
"This has been done completely ignoring the views of the major political parties represented in parliament," the communists said, calling for an all-party meeting on the issue.
Analyst Ashis Nandy of the Centre for Study of Developing Societies (CSDS) told Reuters that the communists had taken the position to protect their political ideology.
"They don't want to be seen as merging their identity into the United Front. They have a different clientele," he said.
The worst the Marxists could do would be to pull out of the United Front, Chopra said.
"The option it could take is to withdraw from the United Front so that it can freely criticise it," he said. But that would not threaten the government, he added.

The CPI-M has 32 lawmakers in the 545-member lower house, or Lok Sabha, short of the number needed to erase the government's majority in parliament. With Congress's 142 votes, the 13-party United Front currently has a comfortable margin.
